People ask me if I’m not too worried about $PL dropping 50%. 

I can tell you I’m very relaxed about the situation. 

First of all because there is nothing fundamentally wrong with Planet. 

Secondly, because I invest in what I call different ‘investment waves’. 

Yes, I have a lot of exposure to the space economy but I’m also exposed to memory, LiDAR, drones, photonics, datacenters, and energy. 

There are some always waves that go up when others come crashing down. 

If I wouldn’t be exposed to space, I think this is an ideal entry point if you want to have exposure. 

If you don’t have exposure to a wave that you want, you need to be aggressive. I wanted exposure to memory, I bought SK Hynix on the first drop during the Iran war at €487. 

SK turned out great from the beginning but a year ago, I wanted exposure to space. During the tariff drop, I bought $PL and $RKLB. Both tumbled 33% after but look where they are now. 

If you want exposure you need to be agressive. Do your research to find the best 2 companies in a wave and don’t doubt when the opportunity comes. 

When you already have exposure you can wait a bit longer. While I’m quite certain that I would have bought Planet if I did not have space exposure today. I think there is a risk that it moves back to the low 20’s. 

If it starts rising again from here, I already have exposure. If it drops to the low $20’s, I add. 

That is why tracking investment waves early is so important. By being aggressive to get exposure, you buy yourself a huge advantage later on.

I believe you can make everything go parabolic in life. It’s just a matter of taking care of the small gains. 

Those gains seem to be negligible in the beginning but if you master the art of small gains, you will soon go parabolic. 

This is the Kaizen philosophy, make sure you improve yourself with 1% everyday. It seems small but if you do this you’ll be x38 times better at the end of the year, x1.444 at the end of year 2. You see the parabolic curve. 

My learning curve in investment started 10 years ago. I invested in low beta companies with paper money. I had no money available to invest with my own money but wanted to be prepared when that day comes. 

I moved from low beta stocks, to dividend stocks, to value stocks, to high growth stocks at the moment. From a paper trader in low beta stocks to the second best investor (behind a certain Serenity) on the platform according to @buzzberg_ai. 

You should try to implement this learning curve in everything you do. Don’t chase the big wins but make the small ones consistent. 

Is it really this easy? 

Off course not, it takes a lot of discipline and focus. 

As I said, your gains will seem negligible. You will have to take small calculated risksk to make sure you keep those daily gains. 

Let me give you kickboxing as an example. You are kicking the opponents thigh 1 time, 2 times, 3 times,… every kick hurts the opponent but with every kick you have to take a calculated risk not to expose yourself. 

Depending on your opponent it can take up to 20 kicks before you start to notice some instability. This can frustrate you, you go for a knock-out, expose yourself and get countered. All those gains for nothing. 

It’s the same with investing, be disciplined. Control your FOMO, you don’t want to lose everything you have build because you take uncalculated risks. 

It seems easy to control this but I’ve played League for a while and here I learned that it’s in the human nature to f* up your smaller gains. Every ones in a while you will throw your gains away and feel frustrated. 

The only thing you can do here is learn from it and move on. There is no future in the past, only lessons to be learned. 

First thing you should do is start. Start today with your parabolic run rather than tomorrow. You’ll be a 38x better human in a year from now.

During the latest earngins call $PL CEO Will Marshall explained that he expects the commercial revenue to be larger than the defense and intelligence revenue in a couple of years. 

At this moment the D&I revenue is 61% of the total revenue of Planet Labs, so what are the solutions Planet provides for the commercial sector? Here are some examples. 

1. Agentic Geospatial AI & LLM Integration
This will probably the biggest factor in the revenue growth of Planet in the next 5 years. The usability of the billions of images that Planet has is limited for none experts. It takes hours to find an answer on what you really need. 

The AI & LLM Integration will completely change this. Take us investors for example, if you are interested in predicting the copper price you can ask: "Show me the stockpile volume changes at global copper mines over the last 90 days". Are you interested in the development of new datacenters of Nebius or IREN for example: "Generate an automated time-series report on datacenter construction in the US". It has endless possibilities for investors but as well for companies. 

At this moment Planet is using with Google who have expertise with Gemini as with Anthropic to implement LLM's into their portal. It's early days, but the scalability of this product will be endless. They will also have a monopoly on this product for the next decade, I don't see any competitor who is close to this kind of solution. 

2. Energy Transition & Climate risk monitoring
The new Tenager satellite mission is specifically designed for enhanced atmospheric gas detection. Planet can offer precise verfiacation of methane leaks and CO2 emissions for energy companies, regulatory compliance bodies, and carbon credit markets. 

Furthermore, using generative AI tools like Planet SuperRes for high-fidelity fire fuel monitoring offers immense value to the insurance industry for pricing localized climate risks.

3. Supply Chain & Maritime Logistics
Expanding their Maritime Domain Awareness products. By combining near-daily optical monitoring with AI-enabled vessel detection, Planet can illuminate dark fleets and monitor port congestion in real-time. This provides critical, asymmetric intelligence for shipping conglomerates, commodity traders, and maritime insurance firms looking to optimize routing and mitigate risk.

4. Advanced Precision Agriculture & Sustainability
Moving beyond basic crop monitoring toward predictive yield analytics and sustainability tracking. By utilizing their high-frequency time-series data, Planet can help global agribusinesses reward farmers for sustainable practices, monitor biodiversity, and track net-zero emission targets across massive agricultural supply chains.

Planet acts as a foundational data supplier for John Deere’s precision agriculture ecosystem. John Deere leverages Planet’s high-frequency, global satellite imagery to power its next-generation agricultural technologies.

Instead of farmers manually scouting massive fields, Planet's data feeds into John Deere's systems (like the John Deere Operations Center) to provide near real-time insights on crop health, moisture levels, and biomass.

This allows the heavy machinery, such as tractors and sprayers, to apply precise amounts of water, fertilizer, or pesticides only exactly where they are needed, rather than blanket-spraying an entire field.

Something I did not emphasize enough in my $PL deep-dive is how bullish the partnership with $GOOGL is. It's an advantage no other company in the industry has. 

A first hurdle for competitors are the massive amounts of data they need to store. They need a cloud provider to help them store and organize the data. Planet has that in Google. Planet's entre operational pipeline is built on and powered by Google Cloud Platform. It was part of the agreement of the Terra bella acquisition of Planet in 2017. 

Planet is building it's own Large Earth Model (LEMs) and Agentic AI workflows. They partner with Google on this as well, they are leveraging Google's Remote Sensing Foundation Model (RSFM) alongside with Gemini-powered reasoning. This integration is what gives the application its agentic capabilities, allowing it to understand a conversational text prompt, autonomously scan Planet's daily global imagery, detect specific objects or changes over time, and synthesize the findings into an analytic report.

Planet refers to this initiative as Queryable Earth or Planetary Intelligence. Instead of training a model purely on internet text, they are essentially training AI on Earth observation data about the physical world. Google's foundation models provide the underlying architecture that translates the user's natural language into complex geospatial queries.

Early 2026 Google and Planet released the highly experimental Project Suncatcher. This is a research initiative exploring the feasibility of running data-center-style computing systems in low Earth orbit. The project aims to see if near-continuous solar power and the vacuum of space can efficiently support energy-intensive artificial intelligence workloads. Planet is leveraging its manufacturing and operational expertise to build and help deploy two demonstration spacecraft for Google, targeted for launch around 2027.

There is no SaaS space company has this massive advantage. These initiatives will blow up the TAM of Planet.

A lot of investors wondering how to profit form the new NVIDIA's 800V HVDC architecture. $WOLF published a great white paper on why SiC is necessary for the pivot. Here is my summary of the paper:

Next generation AI factories require massive amounts of power. Delivering power at 800V DC reduces wiring requirements, improves efficiency, and allows for mu higher GPU density in server racks. 

However the major bottleneck is getting power from the utility grid to the data center. Currently, this relies on conventional medium-voltage (MV) iron-core transformers, which use heavy copper windings and magnetic cores to step down the AC voltage. The massive spike in AI data center construction has caused a supply chain crisis for these traditional transformers, resulting in lead times of up to 3 years.

To bypass this supply chain bottleneck and improve efficiency, engineers are replacing traditional heavy iron-core transformers with Solid-State Transformers (SSTs).

An SST uses solid-state semiconductor devices (power electronics) rather than just copper coils to step down and convert the voltage. It takes the 13.8 - 35 kV AC power from the grid and directly converts it into the 800 VDC required by the AI server racks.

Conventional power switches made of standard Silicon (specifically, Silicon IGBTs - Insulated-Gate Bipolar Transistors) cannot handle the requirements of an SST effectively. They suffer from high switching losses and are limited to low switching frequencies (a few hundred Hertz).

This is where Silicon Carbide (SiC), a wide-bandgap semiconductor, comes in:

- High Switching Frequency: SiC MOSFETs (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistors) can operate at frequencies greater than 10,000 Hz.

- Smaller Magnetics: In transformer design, as switching frequency increases, the physical size of the required magnetic coils and cores decreases. By switching at >10,000 Hz, SiC enables compact, lightweight SSTs that take up a fraction of the floor space of a traditional transformer.

- Thermal Efficiency: Wolfspeed’s SiC achieves 99% conversion efficiency, which reduces the need for heavy thermal cooling systems by 50% compared to Silicon IGBTs.

The article highlights two distinct engineering approaches to building an SST, depending on the blocking voltage of the SiC devices used:

1. Medium-Voltage (MV) SiC (< 5kV blocking voltage)

- Architecture: Because the voltage is lower, engineers must use a multi-level architecture comprising several cascaded converter cells (stacking multiple devices in series) to handle the grid's high voltage.

- Pros: Smaller, highly modular building blocks that are easier to service. Commercially available 3.3kV gate drivers already exist. It also generates a smaller dv/dt (the rate of change of voltage over time), which minimizes Electromagnetic Interference (EMI).

- Cons: Requires complex control algorithms to trigger the series of switches perfectly, and demands precise insulation coordination between the cells.

2. High-Voltage (HV) SiC (> 5kV blocking voltage)

- Architecture: Utilizing Wolfspeed’s advanced 10kV SiC MOSFETs, designers can use a much simpler two-level cell architecture.

- Pros: Vastly simplifies the control scheme and insulation needs because there are fewer cascaded cells.

- Cons: These devices switch with a very high dv/dt, which requires an ultra-low-parasitic design to manage EMI. Furthermore, compatible gate drivers for >3.3kV are rare, often requiring custom development.

In short, the article argues that the rapid expansion of AI requires a fundamental redesign of how power is delivered from the grid. By utilizing 10kV SiC MOSFETs to build Solid-State Transformers, the industry can eliminate massive transformer lead times, achieve higher efficiency, and deliver the specific 800V HVDC power that modern AI clusters require, provided the industry can mature the surrounding ecosystem of high-voltage gate drivers and millisecond-class DC fault clearing protection systems.

Got some questions regarding the Filtronic drop today. I honestly don't know exactly what caused this drop. I see most space stocks are struggling a bit on this green day. 

I've looked a bit deeper into the SpaceX numbers and the only 'issue' that might have caused this drop are the CapEx numbers. 

The CapEx numbers were staggering with $20 billion, wich is great for companies downstream like Filtronic. The only problem here is that we see a rather unexpected shift from using this cash for satellite deployment towards xAI. 

60% of the CapEx ($13 billion of the total $20 billion) has been used on xAI, and the AI division lost around $6.4 billion alone. 

Around $4.18 billion went to starlink and $3.83 billion went to other space themes. In 2024, $6.85 billion went to Starlink. So, it is a drop in CapEx of 39% towards Starlink. 

By prioritizing the AI division instead of the satellite deployment, it could be that some investors are now questioning the forward order flow for hardware suppliers like Filtronic. 

I don't know if this is what caused the sell-off but this is the only possibility I see. 

I also don't think it's a big reason of concern for Filtronic. Yes they rely on SpaceX for their R&D and for 75% of their revenue, but they don't need billions. SpaceX is deciding where to put the CapEx and they are still researching the communication development with Filtronic.

@red1wj Numbers without context are just numbers and context without numbers is just context. Have learned that only when you combine both, you can draw meaningful conclusions.

I see a lot of people completely misinterpreting this graph, as absolute numbers like this basically say nothing on their own.

First of all there is a difference between backlog and orders on hand (ooh). While American companies only need to report the backlog, the ooh tells much more. Your backlog basically has no timeframe, while your ooh only starts when you receive the purchase order. 

If you sign a 10-year frame agreement, you can put all these orders in backlog. But the customer will place several different purchase orders within this frame agreement, so your ooh will be way smaller and on a shorter timeframe. 

You can have a $1 billion backlog over 10-years with only 5% in ooh but also a $200 million backlog over 1-year with 95% in ooh. 

Secondly, I saw some people putting the backlog against the market cap to see which is the best investment. Even with the ooh, this would be completely useless without considering the margins. 

The SaaS model of $PL has way higher margins than $FLY for example. A lower backlog or ooh can result in higher free cash flow. 

Lastly, backlog is not always a positive thing. It all depends on the predictability of your product. In a production environment a backlog can mean a lot of delays and unhappy customers. 

A subscription on the other hand is very predictable and the backlog will always be converted into revenues. 

So, be careful with taking conclusions out of numbers without knowing any context.

Wistron Corp provides the critical networking hardware that connects the end-user to the Starlink satellite constellation. While the satellites handle the space-based infrastructure, WNC focuses on the ground level, manufacturing the routers and network gear essential for the consumer and enterprise terminals.

As Starlink expands its global footprint, the demand for these ground terminals skyrockets. The realities of providing reliable, high-speed internet in diverse environments require robust and precisely engineered networking equipment. WNC has proven to be a core supplier capable of delivering this technology at a massive scale.

This represents a major opportunity tied directly to commercial adoption. A successful SpaceX IPO will inevitably accelerate the global rollout of Starlink services. 3. Compeq Manufacturing
Compeq provides the physical foundation for Starlink's hardware. To make the satellites and ground stations function, highly complex High-Density Interconnect (HDI) printed circuit boards (PCBs) are required, and this Taiwanese specialist has emerged as an absolute core supplier for SpaceX's electronics.

The harsh environment of space and the strict tolerances required for aerospace communication demand incredibly durable and precise electronics. Compeq delivers this reliability at scale, manufacturing the specialized PCBs that are integrated into both the orbiting constellation and the millions of consumer dishes.

This is a direct bet on hardware volume. An IPO capital injection will accelerate the rollout of the satellite network and the manufacturing of end-user terminals to meet global demand. Every new piece of Starlink hardware built directly increases the demand for Compeq's high-end HDI boards.

STM supplies the essential microcontrollers (including the STM32 family), power management ICs, and radio frequency chips. These components are not only found in the LEO satellites but, more importantly, in the millions of ground terminals (dishes) at the end-user level. Listened to the $AMPX earnings yesterday. Needed to sleep about it. Got mixed feelings to be honest. 

The Good

- Revenues keep growing with more than 150% YoY. It looks to slow down a bit QoQ but we saw the same in Q1 last year. Nothing to be worried about here. 

- They secured a contract in China. As explained in the call, China is a very competitive area for battery suppliers. The fact that they were able to secure a contract in that region proves their technology.

- They raised their 2026 forecast with $5 million. Management is confident in growing their revenues due to a backlog from their customers. 

- At this moment in time Amprius got the best battery technology in terms of energy densitiy per kg. I'm not a battery expert, but from the technical reports I can read, Amprius is a clear winner. 

The question marks

- The gross profit margin: Having a moat is something subjective. It often depends on the framework you use. I like to use a more objective approach. If you can grow your revenues and gross profit margin, you have a moat. A clear technology advantage in one of the fastest growing markets, should result in both revenue and gross profit margin growth imo.

The fact that this is not the case this quarter worries me a bit. The fact that they did not give a clear answer on how to raise the margin again, worries me even more. He gave an explanation about one-off costs and some high overhead costs, but nothing to significant imo. 

He also told that they probably lost a couple of % points due to the fact that they are not a multi-million dollar revenue company. That if they would have more revenues, that they would be able to streamline costs and win a couple of % points moving to 24%-25%. While I don't disagree, it's a useless answer. They will not be a multi-million dollar revenue company soon, so they will have to find other ways. 

- Customer concentration: 50% of the revenue comes from 3 main customers. 35% of the revenue goes to the war in Ukraine. I have companies in my portfolio that are for 75% dependant on 1 customer, so I should be able to live with that. It's the fact that they are not able to charge those customers more, that worries me.

Just listened to the $WOLF earnings call. Not the most dynamic call to be honest, but we'll take it. 

There are 2 main things I take away form the earnings call. 

1 - The new go-to-market approach

A market approach always existed out of product lines and product experts. You had certain products sales engineers who were experts in a certain product of the company. They were able to sell 1 product and if the customer needed another product, they needed to send someone else. 

There is a completely new approach now, the applications approach. I see this change happening in my professional life. Wolfspeed is also implementing this. Your sales engineers are now application experts, they know exactly what the application needs and can give feedback to the product experts who often work away from the customer. 

the big positive of this is you can actually target the customer needs and give feedback to the product experts. It gives better customer satisfaction and makes your R&D more customer related as well. 

We can already see the first signs of this approach with the new 10kV MOSFET and TOLT portfolio for AI. 

2 - Debt

Wolfspeed has been able to reduce its debt significantly. They raised around $476 M via private placement. They used a combination of new convertable notes, normal stock and pre-funded warrants. 

They used this cash to reduce their most expensive debt. They reduced this post with 43%. The total debt was reduced from $2.3B to $1.7B. The estimation is that they would save around $63 Million of yearly interest. 

The first big debt relief is now in 2030. So, the most important part from all this is that I don't expect further dilution in the near-term. The only possible dilution would now come from the convertible notes. This dilution will only start if the stock would surge a lot. So, this is not too bad for existing shareholders. 

3 - Other Things

The main focus was to get rid of the most expensive debt. With Wolfspeed showing that they are capable of get rid of it in combination with a rising stock price, they expect a rerate of the stock. Wolfspeed is still very cheap in comparison with competitors, so a re-rate is not impossible. 

The new focus will now be on free cash flow. It's a good approach in my opnion, I often look more at the free cash flow than at the EBITDA. Less accounting tricks possible with the free cash flow.

I initiated a position in $WOLF yesterday. I bought the stock at $36. 

I discovered Wolfspeed as they are an indirect supplier of Filtronic. The space communication tech is rapidly developing. Filtronic is buidling GaN on SiC E-band and V-band amps. I predict that this market will grow rapidly in the upcoming years. 

Filtronic is buying the GaN on SiC amps from $MTSI. MACOM bought this division form Wolfspeed. $WOLF sold this division in order to make sure they can be entirely focused on their SiC division. 

They still have a sales agreement with MACOM and are selling their 200mm SiC wafers to MACOM. While most competitors are still refining the 150mm SiC wafers, Wolfspeed is already developing 300mm SiC wafers. 

300mm SiC wafers are a game changer for datacenters and for space. 300mm SiC wafers provide 4x the surface area of 150 mm SiC wafers. This geometry yields vastly more chips per wafer and reduces edge waste, drastically lowering the manufacturing cost per device through economies of scale. 

$WOLF is currently valued at ~$1.7B with an EV of ~$2.6B and ~$800m debt. The market is giving zero premium for future growth or IP. Being the main innovator in the SiC space, I think the market will soon start to give a premium again. 

Their main sales market now is the EV market. Which is unreliable and often cyclical. I understand the market does not want to give a premium for this. But with the change to 200mm SiC wafers and 300mm SiC wafers, they enter the datacenter and space market. 

Wolfspeed is not without risk. The company basically went bankrupt in June 2025. They needed protection from chapter 11. They have negative free cash flow with ~$800m debt. They need to invest heavily in R&D for the 300mm SiC wafers and got some competition. 

They needed government funding under the chips and science act, securing a first $750m with the possibility on another $1B. 

I’m willing to take this risk as I believe 300mm SiC wafers will be a real game changer. Even with the 200mm SiC wafers, they were able to grow the datacenter segment with 50%. This segment will become more and more important for them. The market is not pricing this in at all.

That's an interesting discussion. The problem is that RF-SOI is extremely inefficient at the frequencies of the E-band and V-band. To produce 50-100W of total power, an RF-SOI array would drain the all the power of the satellite's solar panels. That electrical inefficiency would also create a massive amount of total waste heat.

Dissipating heat in the vacuum of space is an enormous problem. Filtronic fixes this by growing GaN on Silicon Carbide (SiC), utilizing a thermal conductivity of 390 to 490 W/mK. This allows them to rapidly pull the intense heat away from the transistor and into the satellite's primary radiators.

Ultimately, at these mmWave frequencies, GaN is simply much more efficient with the limited electricity on a satellite and produces less total heat to manage.

"The Proprietary 100-Point Execution and Integrity Rubric
To cleanly separate transparent, executing leaders from chronic under-deliverers in the high-growth equity space, the following proprietary 100-point framework evaluates management strictly on qualitative, auditable behaviors. Traditional profitability metrics are entirely excluded. The framework is divided into five weighted categories, each with specific instructions on where analysts can source the required data.

Category 1: The "Say-Do" Ratio (Maximum 30 Points)
The Say-Do Ratio tracks the historical reliability of management's public promises versus their actual execution.12 In pre-profit companies, trust is the only currency; if management cannot accurately forecast their own engineering and sales timelines, their financial projections are entirely worthless.

Metrics & Scoring:
The category is divided into Product Delivery (15 points) and Guidance Accuracy (15 points). Analysts must award full points for Product Delivery if the commercialization timelines, partnership integrations, or manufacturing milestones stated in investor presentations from 24 to 36 months prior were met on schedule. Analysts must deduct 5 points for every major product delay, timeline revision, or quiet abandonment of a previously hyped product line. For Guidance Accuracy, award full points if the company consistently meets or slightly beats its own forward-looking revenue, backlog, or customer acquisition guidance. Deduct 10 points for chronic downward revisions, repeatedly missed targets, or the sudden withdrawal of future guidance without a catastrophic macroeconomic catalyst.

Data Sourcing:
Analysts must access the company's investor relations website or the SEC EDGAR database to locate archival investor presentations and initial public offering (or SPAC) prospectuses from 24 to 36 months prior. Extract the specific timelines promised in those documents and cross-reference them against the current year's Form 10-K "Management's Discussion and Analysis" (MD&A). Furthermore, analysts must compare historical stated deadlines against the actual press releases announcing commercial availability to calculate the exact length of any delays.

Category 2: Communication & Transparency (Maximum 20 Points)
This category measures the integrity, clarity, and psychological tone of executive communication. It assesses whether management treats investors as intelligent partners or as targets for manipulation.

Metrics & Scoring:
This category evaluates Clarity and Accountability (10 points) and the Absence of Promotional Jargon (10 points). Award maximum points for Clarity and Accountability if executives provide clear, direct, and mathematically precise answers during the Q&A sessions of earnings calls. Deduct 5 points if management consistently blames macro-environmental factors for missing idiosyncratic, company-specific goals, or if they exhibit defensive, evasive behavior when pressed by bearish analysts. Award points for the Absence of Promotional Jargon if press releases are highly technical, customer-centric, and data-driven. Deduct up to 10 points for excessive reliance on market buzzwords, the hyping of non-binding "Memorandums of Understanding" (MOUs) as guaranteed revenue, or prematurely announcing unfinalized contracts that subsequently fall through.

Data Sourcing:
Analysts must read the transcripts of the last four quarterly earnings calls. The prepared remarks should be largely ignored; the analysis must focus specifically on the Q&A section, scrutinizing management's real-time responses to adversarial or critical analyst questions. Additionally, analysts must search SEC 8-K filings for any retracted statements, "clarifications" forced by regulatory bodies, or public apologies for leaking confidential client data.

Category 3: Capital & Dilution Discipline (Maximum 25 Points)
For pre-profit companies, managing the share structure is just as important as managing the product.4 A brilliant technology will still result in zero shareholder returns if the equity is diluted into oblivion before commercialization.

Metrics & Scoring:
This section evaluates Dilution Restraint (10 points), Stock-Based Compensation (10 points), and Balance Sheet Management (5 points). Award full points for Dilution Restraint if the outstanding share count has grown by less than 5% annually, or if any major dilution was strictly tied to immediately accretive M&A activity. Deduct up to 10 points for "death spiral" dilution—frequent, desperate equity raises featuring heavy warrant coverage without any corresponding revenue growth. For Stock-Based Compensation (SBC), award points if SBC is a reasonable, single-digit fraction of total operational expenses. Deduct points heavily if executive SBC continues to scale upward while the stock price declines, or if SBC is mathematically larger than the company's gross revenue. Award points for Balance Sheet Management if the company has successfully secured non-dilutive capital (grants, low-interest debt) or maintains a multi-year cash runway that negates the need for immediate equity offerings.

Data Sourcing:
Analysts must utilize financial charting tools or standard 10-K filings to track the "Shares Outstanding" metric over a trailing 5-year period to calculate the exact compound annual growth rate of the dilution. Review the Statement of Cash Flows in the 10-K to isolate Stock-Based Compensation and measure it as a percentage of both total cash burn and total revenue. Finally, review the capitalization table in the footnotes of the financial statements to identify toxic derivative warrant liabilities or convertible debt death spirals.

Category 4: Founder-Led & Insider Alignment (Maximum 15 Points)
This category assesses whether management shares the same financial fate as retail and institutional investors, embodying the "skin in the game" philosophy.

Metrics & Scoring:
Evaluate Insider Ownership & Buying (10 points) and Planned vs. Opportunistic Sales (5 points). Award points for high insider ownership (e.g., greater than 10% of outstanding shares) and consistent, open-market buying by the C-suite and Board of Directors. Deduct points for heavy, continuous open-market selling. For the second metric, deduct 5 points immediately if insider selling occurs in the weeks prior to negative news, contract cancellations, or missed earnings. Award points if all insider sales are strictly executed via pre-planned Rule 10b5-1 programs that were established months in advance of the sale.

Data Sourcing:
Analysts must analyze SEC Form 4 filings (or equivalent insider trading disclosures in foreign jurisdictions). The analyst must meticulously differentiate between routine option execution/tax selling (which is standard and acceptable when executed via 10b5-1 plans) and opportunistic, discretionary block selling by C-suite executives seeking to front-run bad news.

Category 5: Strategic Focus (Maximum 10 Points)
This measures the company's ability to stay on course, defending its economic moat rather than chasing the latest technological fad to generate short-term retail interest.

Metrics & Scoring:
Evaluate Core Competency Alignment (10 points). Award full points if R&D and capital expenditure are aggressively deployed into defending and expanding the core product suite. Deduct 10 points if the company repeatedly pivots its entire business model to chase trending sectors—such as pivoting from telecommunications, to blockchain, to EV infrastructure, to artificial intelligence—without ever establishing meaningful market share or revenue in any of the prior iterations.

Data Sourcing:
Analysts must track the "Business Overview" section of the Form 10-K over three consecutive years to detect major shifts in the stated Total Addressable Market (TAM) or core technology focus. Compare the product lines emphasized in the current year's presentation against the product lines emphasized three years prior."

Starshield might be the best earth observation platform for governments. 

Still $PL surged 50% in their Defense & Intelligence segment.  

Here is a breakdown on why that was possible and why I think it will surge further.

1. The Power of Unclassified Intelligence:
SpaceX’s Starshield is an absolute beast, but it is highly classified and built almost exclusively for the U.S. military. If the U.S. or NATO needs to share intelligence with non-cleared global allies, or expose adversarial troop movements to the public, they cannot use Starshield without exposing secret spy capabilities. 

$PL provides commercial, unclassified data that is instantly shareable on the world stage. Governments need both. 
 
2. Broad-Area Monitoring vs. Targeted Spying:
Classified spy satellites are expensive and in incredibly high demand. Intelligence agencies use Planet’s daily, global scans to monitor massive geographic areas on a budget. When $PL's baseline data shows something suspicious, like a new military base or border buildup, the government then tasks its classified assets like Starshield to take a closer, highly targeted look. Planet frees up the heavy hitters.  

3. Moving From Pixels to Answers:
Defense agencies are drowning in raw satellite imagery and don't have enough human analysts to review it all. Planet shifted its business model to address this, notably partnering with NVIDIA to build GPU-native AI engines into its data pipeline. $PL is no longer just selling pictures; they are selling automated alerts. 

If an adversary moves fighter jets to a contested airfield, Planet’s AI flags it instantly.  

Why I Think It Will Surge Further 
• A Massive, Locked-In Backlog: $PL just reported a backlog of over $900 million which is a 79% year-over-year increase that is nearly three times their current annual revenue. The defense demand isn't just theoretical, the money is already committed.  

• The Sovereign Space Boom: International allies realize they can't rely 100% on U.S. classified intelligence. Buying a subscription to $PL gives nations like Germany and Sweden their own dedicated eyes in the sky without needing to spend billions building and launching their own satellite constellations.  

• The Profitability Turning Point: After years of cash burn, $PL just achieved its first full fiscal year of adjusted EBITDA profitability ($15.5 million) and positive free cash flow. They now have the solid financial foundation required to scale their next-generation Pelican (high-resolution) and Tanager (hyperspectral) fleets.  

Starshield is going to completely dominate the classified realm, but open-source Earth intelligence is officially a booming, highly profitable sector. Don't sleep on $PL.

I have to admit something. 

I bought $SIVE at SEK 11 on the 19th of March. 
I sold $SIVE at SEK 8.14 on the 20th of March. 

My mistake cost me €600. Let me explain, so you can learn form it as well. 

On big projects, I often join my sales engineers to make sure we secure the deal. March wasn't a great month for my business line and we had a final conversation for a big project. This would make or break my entire month. 

There was a lot of pressure from above to make sure we close this deal. Long story short, we didn't close the deal. The customer chose a cheaper, less qualitative short-term solution. 

Back in my car, I was furious. I felt my sales engineer pushed the customer too much into a certain solution, closing the options for him. I knew there was going to be a difficult conversation on why we'd lost the deal. 

Fuming as I was in my car, I opened X. The first tweet I saw presented it to me as the holy grail. A tweet from, back them a far lesser known, Serenity about a certain new stock; $SIVE. 

He already made some good calls, but as I was in a very busy period, I never had the time to do my own research on the companies and I never just blindly someone else.

At least, I never had blindly followed someone else. Until now. 2 minutes later, I bought a 2-3% allocation in Sivers. 

I always scream that blindly following people is the biggest mistake an investor can make and that you always have to do your own research to build conviction. Yet here I was, rejecting my own rules. 

Of course, I immediately had a bad feeling about the transaction and luckily for me I only bought a very small portion. Normally I buy at minimum a 5% allocation, this time I bought less. 

Next day, I had the shit conversation with my gm and the divisional president. The conversation left me frustrated. I opened my broker app later that day and what did I see, $SIVE was down almost 30%. 

If I did my research and if I knew what I was holding, this would have been a golden opportunity to add some to my position. But this time, I had no clue what I was holding. I panicked and sold my position. I'm probably the only one who made a loss on Sivers since March, but I learned my lesson. 

I have to accept that I do my research just for fun as my full commitment is to my job. Because of that, I will miss opportunities. There are periods that I just can't do a lot of research and that's ok, I should not be chasing hypes during this period. 

I try to bring you guys value by doing research on new stocks like $PL, $INV, Filtronic, $AMPX,... I don't get joy anyway in doing the 17th deep-dive in the same stock, so why should I chase that hype? 

I'm up 50% YTD with a unique portfolio, I'm transparent and try to give you guys as much information as possible. I'm proud of that and will continue on this route. 

I did not post anything on $SIVE because I did not do any research and could not post any information. I learned my lesson now. 

You will have shit days at work like me, feeling the urge to chase every opportunity. But please calm down and know you don't have to buy every stock you see on here. Do your own research, you'll be proud of what you can achieve.

Major players like SpaceX and $AMZN have already secured FCC approval for thousands of V-band satellites, while companies like Astra Space and Boeing are actively exploring their own constellations.

Currently, only a few suppliers can manufacture the necessary V-band GaN amplifiers. However, they produce expensive, unpackaged, and low-volume aerospace parts. 

This creates a massive bottleneck for networks like Starlink and Project Kuiper, which rely on millions of cheap, ready-to-use modules.

To solve this, SpaceX is funding Filtronic to transform these raw GaN chips into affordable, mass-manufactured components for consumer hardware.

Notably, Filtronic is also running a separate multi-million dollar R&D project with an unnamed US partner, which many speculate could be Amazon.

So, why Filtronic? 

Even if a company acquires a bare V-band GaN chip, they still face the massive engineering challenge of wiring, packaging, and cooling it so it doesn't melt a plastic satellite dish during an Arizona summer.

Filtronic’s core expertise lies in advanced RF packaging and thermal management. They excel at turning raw, heat-intensive chips into rugged, highly efficient plug-and-play modules that integrate perfectly into phased-array antennas.

If Filtronic can successfully adapt its proven E-band expertise into this emerging V-band market, it is positioned to capture a virtual monopoly in a rapidly growing, multi-billion-dollar industry.

Historically, Earth observation (EO) smallsats have relied on X-band radios to downlink the pictures they take to ground stations, and S-band or UHF for basic telemetry and commanding (TT&C).

By equipping the Pelican-7 satellite with Ka-Band and C-Band antennas, $PL is fundamentally changing the satellite's data pipe.

• Ka-Band (High Frequency, High Bandwidth): Ka-band operates at a much higher frequency than X-band. In radio communications, higher frequencies allow for significantly wider bandwidths, which translates to much faster data transfer rates.

The technical impact: Pelican satellites are designed to take very high-resolution imagery (up to 30cm). High-resolution images result in massive file sizes. Ka-band allows Planet to download gigabytes of imagery to a ground station in a fraction of the time it would take using legacy systems.

• C-Band: While lower frequency than Ka-band, C-band is highly resistant to "rain fade" (signal degradation due to weather). It provides a highly reliable, robust channel for commanding the satellite, ensuring that tasking orders (telling the satellite where to look) are received instantly and reliably, regardless of weather conditions over the ground station.

In the defense, intelligence, and financial sectors, an image is only valuable if you get it quickly. $BKSY has historically held a strong edge in latency, heavily marketing their ability to task a satellite and deliver an image in under 90 minutes. 

Planet's upgrade to Ka-band directly targets this. By downloading massive images faster, Planet can significantly reduce the time between when an image is snapped and when it appears on a customer's screen.

Fabrinet is essentially the manufacturing backbone for the entire optical industry. Companies like Lumentum and Coherent pour billions into R&D to design cutting-edge lasers and transceivers, but they outsource the actual building, testing, and packaging to $FN. This allows them to scale without spending billions on their own factories.

Furthermore, $FN is already manufacturing optical cables directly for $NVDA. Nvidia designs its own proprietary Active Optical Cables (AOCs) to connect its GPUs within server racks. Instead of buying these from a middleman, Nvidia goes straight to Fabrinet to build them.

AI data centers are entirely dependent on moving data between thousands of GPUs instantly. The bottleneck is optical networking. Because Fabrinet manufactures these ultra-precise, high-margin optical components, they hold a highly specialized and lucrative position.

The ceiling on $FN might be lower than the volatile designers like $LITE and $COHR, but for investors who want a safer route into photonics, $FN is perfectly positioned. We know photonics is a bottleneck, but $FN is the bottleneck within the bottleneck.

Earnings were not spectacular for $POET, but they have never been. The first (apart from NRE's) revenue is expected in the second half of 2026.

The most interesting financial story of the earnings is that they now have a cash balance of $313.4 million. The total liabilities are $40 million. So, with a market cap of $888 million, your downside is limited. Investors are always willing to pay on top of the book value.

The upside is on the other hand has unlimited potential. POET Technologies possess a highly unique, proprietary solution to the optical alignment bottleneck through its POET Optical Interposer. 

This global silicon photonics market as of 2025 has an estimated TAM of $2.86 billion. This TAM is expected to grow to $28.75 billion by 2034.

However POET is still in pre-revenue phase, it is not an unwritten book. They first hit public markets in 2008 under the name Opel International. At that time, they were focused on solar panels and solar tracking systems. As they realized that the solar market was a race to the bottom, they changed strategy.

In 2012, the company rebranded to POET Technologies and they started to focus on the chip industry. They spent years trying to create a monolithic chip that could do the job of both electricity and light. They proved this could work in lab but failed to scale the idea.

In 2015, they hired a new CEO Dr. Suresh Venkatesan. They pivoted toward the optical interposer. Instead of making one giant chip, they built a bridge that allows existing electronic chips and optical (light) chips to be snapped together easily. This bridge took nearly a decade of engineering, ensuring more than 100 patents, and setting up complex supply chains.

After a decade they look ready to move from an R&D phase towards real revenue. They recently secured a $5 million initial order for 800G optical engines and they are expected to ship more than 30,000 optical engines this year across both high-speed and high-power segments. 

If they are able to scale up production this time, you are looking at a $1 billion company revolutionizing a multibillion-dollar industry. If they completely fail, you are looking at a 50% loss max imo.

Management is not very transparent about the progress at the moment, so it can feel a bit like you are blindfolded on a bumpy ride. But with this upside, it's a risk I'm willing to take.

$SIVE looks like the only investable option out of the pack in my opinion. Yes, gross profit margins are still shrinking but at least the revenues are growing. 

Main reason I find for the dropping margins is a change in revenue mix. The standard products are the high-margin products, while the custom-made products have a significantly lower margin. 

In 2023, management promised to increase the high-margin products from 30% of the revenue to over 80% by 2026. For the full year of 2025, the high margin products accounted for 28.2%.... So quite far from the 80% target. 

The new target is to move to 65% within the next 2 years. The big pipeline should make this possible. The standard product pipeline grew by 90%, so it looks like the shift is happening. 

Which bottleneck do they serve? 

$SIVE serves two primary bottlenecks:

1. The AI Compute Bottleneck: As AI models scale into the trillions of parameters, traditional copper-based electrical routing suffers from insurmountable signal degradation and thermal inefficiencies. 

Sivers solves this by providing the proprietary Indium Phosphide (InP) external light sources (ELS) essential for Silicon Photonics (SiPh) and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO). This transition to light-based data transfer offers a 90% reduction in interconnect power consumption. 

2. The SATCOM and 5G/6G Beamforming Bottleneck: The deployment of mega-constellations of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites requires terrestrial ground terminals to maintain connectivity with fast-moving targets. 

Sivers addresses this by providing advanced millimeter-wave (mmWave) Radio Frequency Integrated Circuits (RFICs) and electronically steerable arrays that deliver unrivaled energy efficiency and low-latency beam steering.

Do they have a monopoly? 

$SIVE does not have an absolute monopoly. They operate within a highly supply-constrained niche oligopoly for specific high-power DFB laser arrays capable of surviving the extreme thermal environments of Co-Packaged Optics.

In the Photonics division addressing the AI datacenter bottleneck, Sivers survives thanks to their extreme specialization. The focus on customized DFB laser arrays rather than competing with the massive scale of the incumbents, they are able to grow revenues. 

Sivers Semiconductors explicitly avoids competing directly with optical giants like $LITE and $COHR on standard, high-volume optical products. 

Lumentum and Coherent possess immense manufacturing scale and dominate the market for traditional optical transceivers, with Lumentum currently holding a near-monopoly on supplying EML lasers for the 1.6T transition.

Instead of battling these multi-billion-dollar incumbents on standard products, Sivers competes and secures its own high margins through extreme specialization. 

The company focuses fiercely on providing highly customized, high-power Distributed Feedback (DFB) laser arrays (such as 8x, 16x, and 32x arrays) rather than broad systems. These specialized arrays are specifically tuned and optimized for non-hermetic, flip-chip integration directly into nascent Silicon Photonics (SiPh) and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) ecosystems.

While standard optical transceivers are highly commoditized, the specific market for 100mW+ continuous-wave DFB laser arrays capable of surviving the extreme thermal environments of CPO integration is severely supply-constrained. 

Because demand for these high-precision external light sources vastly outstrips supply, Sivers retains significant pricing power, which protects its long-term target of 65%.

Why is it so difficult to grow the high margin products to 65% of the revenue? 

Sivers doesn't sell off-the-shelf commodities. They are integrating entirely new physical architectures into the proprietary systems of Fortune 100 hyperscalers.

This design phase takes anywhere from 3 to 5 years. During this time, Sivers is paid via Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE) fees to customize, test, and tweak the prototypes. You can have all the pricing power in the world, but if the customer is still in year three of a four-year testing phase, they simply aren't going to buy a million units yet.

Transitioning from making 5,000 flawless prototypes in a lab to manufacturing 5,000,000 flawless chips in a commercial fab is a nightmare of physics and engineering. 

If they rush the volume ramp before the manufacturing yield is perfected, they will produce defective chips, which instantly destroys their gross margins. They have to scale deliberately to ensure that when they do hit that 65% product mix, the chips actually work and the 65% gross margin target holds up.

Conclusion
It's an interesting company that is mainly paid by NRE fees. If they can pivot these R&D services into real product sales, they should be able to finally grow gross profit margins and revenues together.

The algorithm is the investor's worst enemy. 

It feeds you confirmation bias as it shows you exactly what you want to read. 

The confirmation bias is one of the biggest pitfalls of an investor. 

The confirmation bias is the cognitive tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information that confirms your pre-existing beliefs or hypotheses, while disregarding contradictory evidence.

All humans suffer from the confirmation bias. Once you take a stand on a certain stock, you tend to look for information that confirms your stand. You tend to ignore the information that contradicts your stand. 

The algorithm does not help. Every bullish post you like on $IREN (for example) will push the algorithm to show you more bullish posts on the stock. 

After a while, you will only see bullish posts. Once in a while, the algorithm will push a bearish one through. You will see this as the one bearish post among the dozens of bullish posts. 

I aim to do the opposite. I search for tweets that are bearish on the stocks I love. I read the arguments and see if I can give counterarguments on the spot. You don't have to post these, you can do it for yourself. 

You will be 10x the investor you are today, if you start reading the opinions of investors whose ideas are conflicting with your stand. Your mind will be more open and you'll learn more about your stock than ever before. 

So feed the algorithm with likes and time on posts that might conflict with your own vision. You'll be surprised with the results.

Here is my thesis:

Traditional lidar relies on analog architectures requiring highly complex manual calibration, meaning one unit of cost equals one unit of revenue. Ouster completely bypassed this by pioneering a fully digital architecture utilizing consumer-grade SPADs and VCSELs integrated into custom silicon.

Because adding resolution simply requires printing denser arrays on silicon, their costs do not scale linearly with performance. This pure volume leverage drove Q4 gross profit margins to a staggering 60.23%.

2. Digital IP & Sensor Fusion
Following mergers with Velodyne and Sense Photonics, Ouster consolidated the foundational IP of the sector, holding over 350 patents globally. 

Furthermore, their recent $35 million acquisition of StereoLabs integrates visual cameras and AI edge compute directly with their lidar. While competitors struggle to scale single sensors, Ouster is offering a plug-and-play multimodal Physical AI stack.

3. Financial Stability
While the lidar sector is littered with bankruptcies—most notably Luminar's Chapter 11 filing in late 2025—Ouster boasts an incredibly fortified balance sheet.

Cash & Equivalents: A massive liquidity position of approximately $211 million.

Debt: Virtually zero, having successfully paid off its revolving credit facility.

They are not desperate for cash. Yhey are playing the long game and consolidating while legacy competitors starve.

4. Quality of Revenue
Ouster isn't sitting around waiting for passenger robotaxis. They target immediate ROI verticals like industrial automation, robotics, and smart infrastructure.

Consistent Growth: They have achieved a 5-year revenue CAGR of 55.01% and shipped over 25,000 sensor units in 2025.

Recurring Software: Their software-attached bookings, driven by the Gemini and BlueCity platforms, doubled in 2025.

5. Most importantly: Regulatory Tailwinds
Chinese competitors like Hesai currently dominate global automotive volume. However, the U.S. SAFE LiDAR Act aims to systematically phase out foreign adversary lidar from domestic critical infrastructure and defense supply chains. 

This legislation creates an artificial, multi-billion-dollar market vacuum in the U.S., paving the way for Ouster to capture an estimated 35% U.S. market share in a neutral scenario.

6. Valuation disconnect
I calculated 3 scenario's for Ouster, Inc.

The main difference between the 3 scenario's is the FCF margin of Ouster, the U.S. TAM, and the amount of US market share they can capture. 

About 66% of the revenues of Ouster now come from the US. market. I project this to become around 80% when the LiDAR act starts. I only projected an estimate of the US market in my projections.

I projected my FCF margins on other sectos that provide AI-hardware but in a more mature phase. In sectors with high competition the lowest FCF-margin I could find is 10%. If they become a real monoply the margin could be as high as 35%. But I don't expect this so, I took 28% in the bull case. 

$OUST now already has a market share of 14% in the US. Different outlets expect this to become between 30% and 40% after the act.

I used a desired return of 10% and a terminal growth of 3%.

I think $OUST is a rare opportunity into a fast growing TAM. I think a worst-case scenario is already priced in and a bull case is certainly not impossible to reach.

No need for panicking, no need for selling your high conviction assets.

1. Structural Buffers in the Global Oil Market
In the latest few years, the global energy market has developed significantly. Most countries now have built-in shock absorbers. 

Record US Oil Production: The United States is currently pumping more oil than any country in history. This alone serves as a buffer for the global energy market, reducing the absolute need for Middle Eastern oil and capping potential price explosions to $150, $200, or even $250 per barrel.

OPEC's Safety Margin: OPEC+ countries, especially Saudi Arabia, are currently holding back millions of barrels of oil per day through voluntary cuts in their output to prop up prices. If a genuine supply shortage were to occur, this safety margin can be rapidly activated to restore order to the global energy market.

Demand-Driven Pricing vs. Supply Panic: When oil prices rise today, it is often a reflection of a strong global economy (particularly in the US) demanding more energy, rather than a panic over supply shortages. For stock markets, a robust economy is always good news, which offsets the bad news of a rise in energy prices.

2. Financial and Economic Resilience
The overall economic environment has also adjusted to high energy prices, making companies and governments less likely to panic.

The End of Interest Rate Panic: In the last few years, because of high energy prices, inflation has risen exponentially. In response, interest rates have been raised significantly. Today, however, overall inflation has cooled down. Investors believe that governments have overall inflation under control. This means that even in a temporary increase in oil and LNG prices, interest rates are not likely to be raised, which would have a devastating effect on markets.

Corporate Pricing Power: Large corporations have surprised us with their skill in transferring high energy costs and other rising costs to consumers without sacrificing corporate earnings. As long as corporate earnings are high, there is no need to panic.

Sophisticated Hedging Strategies: Large energy-intensive companies have learned valuable lessons from previous energy crises. These companies have now adopted sophisticated financial strategies to protect themselves from rising energy prices. These strategies involve locking in long-term energy prices. This provides them with a financial shield against rising prices.

3. The Geopolitical and Strategic Deterrents

Economic Suicide for Iran: Although Iran often threatens to use this Strait as a geopolitical tool, shutting off the Strait would mean economic suicide for them. Iran heavily depends on exporting oil through this very same Strait, primarily to China.

Regional Economic Destruction: The Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, and UAE, rely almost entirely on the Strait of Hormuz for their economic revenues. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz would completely destabilize the economy of the Middle East; hence, there is tremendous pressure on keeping the flow of oil and gas going, irrespective of any tensions.

The ATM trend continues: Following $IREN's massive $6B ATM offering filing, $AAOI has followed suit, filing for its own $250M ATM.

Do you know what an ATM actually is, and why it should concern you as a shareholder?

Let me explain
An At-The-Market (ATM) offering is a mechanism a publicly traded company uses to raise cash by creating new shares of stock and selling them directly into the open market at the current trading price.

Imagine a company that owns a glass safe. In the safe is exactly $10. The company has 10 shares at the moment, all trading at $1. If you own 1 share, you have the right to 10% of what is in the vault (so, $1). It is an open market, so everyone can see what is in the safe. 

The company now wants to do an ATM of $5, which means they will be looking for 5 new shareholders to put $1 extra in the safe. If 5 new shareholders put an extra $5 in the safe, the safe will be worth $15 and there are now 15 shares. Still all worth $1. You now own 6.67% of a $15 company instead of 10% of a $10 company. 

So, if the math balances perfectly, why does the stock price almost always drop?

1. True, for the first part of the explanation we can stay with our virtual safe company. Why would a person pay $1 to get a $1 share in return? There might be a risk that the safe gets stolen. He wants a return. So to convince new investors, you will probably have to sell the new shares at $0.95. This has an immediate negative impact on the existing shareholders. 

The more shareholders you need to find, the lower the convincing price will become. When the price drops, existing shareholders might want to sell as well. This can become a negative spiral. 

2. Another immediate impact is that the EPS will drop. Let's say that after the money is 1 year in the safe, it will return $0.1. So in the beginning the $10 will return $1 each year. Every investor will get $0.1 and the EPS will be 0.1. 

Now there is $15 in the safe, but the last $5 will not return money for another year. The $1 realized profit will now have to be divided over 15 shares. The EPS will automatically drop to 0.067. 

3. For the final negative part, we need to leave the safe example. In a real company, the value is different for every investor. The share price is a constant battle between supply and demand. With an ATM, the supply obviously increases while the demand might not. 

The demand could increase as well, as investors might think that the board might do great things with the new money. But when the ATM is big, the pressure of the constant new supply might be overwhelming. 

Conclusion
So, the share price certainly does not have to come down with a small ATM. If investors trust the company to achieve high returns with the fresh money, the ATM might be a great decision. 

But the 3 consequences explained here will put constant pressure on that stock price. Convincing new shareholders, a lower EPS and a constant new supply of shares might be costly for existing shareholders.

Last Monday, I took a position in $POET at $6.52.

Here is my business case

As artificial intelligence models continue to grow in complexity, the conventional copper cables used to transport data within a hyperscale data center are no longer sufficient, having reached their physical limits in term of bandwidth, latency, and thermal dissipation.

The data transmission industry is in a state of change to a more efficient method of data transmission using light. The conventional method of photonics manufacturing is a labor-intensive and time-consuming process that requires microscopic lenses to be manually adjusted to achieve optimal light transmission. This process is naturally limiting in terms of efficiency and is not conducive to a high-volume manufacturing scenario.

$POET breaks all of this convention with their semiconductorization of photonics.

Wafer-Scale Passive Alignment: The POET Optical Interposer makes use of conventional complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor processes to etch waveguides and alignment features directly into a silicon wafer.

The LEGO Method: Bare die components, which include lasers and electronic chips, are flip-chip assembled onto the interposer using automated pick-and-place machinery. This allows components to be snapped together automatically, eliminating the active alignment bottleneck.

Architectural Superiority: The POET method is far superior to conventional methods due to their ability to operate at a massive wafer scale, reducing the overall Bill of Materials by a significant amount and minimizing overall assembly time. Additionally, their highly integrated optical engines consume much less power overall, saving up to 6-8 watts per module individually.

Product Innovation: The POET flagship product, the 1.6T Teralight engine, is a highly innovative optical engine. It incorporates a unique design utilizing four 2x200G Electro-absorption Modulated Lasers, effectively cutting in half the number of discrete laser chips.

Financial De-risking and Structural Health
The biggest risk for early-stage hardware companies is running out of capital. POET has successfully neutralized this near-term liquidity risk.

Between October 2025 and January 2026, the company successfully raised a combined $225 million via institutional private placements and registered direct offerings.

This big capital injection bolstered the balance sheet to ~$350 million in cash and marketable securities.

The company maintains a clean capital structure, with almost no debt obligations.

This pristine balance sheet provides a multi-yea runway to execute its commercial ramp without the threat of further dilutive financing.

Commercial Validation and Valuation Realism
POET's technical roadmap is  developing into commercial reality. The company recently secured a $5m production order for its 800G Infinity optical engines, scheduled for delivery to a leading systems integrator in the second half of 2026. 

POET is also embedded with global manufacturing heavyweights such as Foxconn Interconnect Technology and Luxshare Tech, alongside strategic partnerships with component leaders like Semtech and Mitsubishi Electric.

A rigorous Reverse Discounted Cash Flow analysis underscores the immense upside potential relative to POET's $1.04 billion market capitalization.

To strictly justify its current enterprise value, POET has to reach a Free Cash Flow of $117.39m by the year 2036.

Assuming a conservative 15% Free Cash Flow margin, they should reach an annual top-line revenue requirement of around $782.6m by 2036.

The silicon photoincs market is projected to be $28.75b by 2034. POET only needs to capture around 2.7% of this market to justify its current valuation.

Conclusion
POET Technologies is a premier high-reward investment for the upcoming AI supercycle. The company offers a disruptive, legally defensible, and structurally protected hardware platform that solves the most pressing physical bottleneck in modern AI network scaling. 

While manufacturing yield execution remains the primary risk, the massive liquidity buffer and definitive validation from tier-one industry partners heavily skew this binary setup toward immense upside potential.

Last year I shared some research on $HIMS and why I think they are ideally positioned for a huge next pharma wave. (yes, they are still down 25% since I shared the research, but it's about the thesis).

It is scientifically proven that GLP-1 helps with cardiovascular health, kidney diseases, addiction, neurological conditions, sleep apnea, fatty liver, fertility, and even more conditions.

So why is it still mainly seen as an obesity drug?

The GLP-1 production is now regulated by 2 main players, $LLY and $NVO. They both own patents that prevent other companies from starting GLP-1 production. This means that both of those companies have huge pricing power.

The pricing power is a simple supply/demand principle here. The supply is limited, so the higher the demand, the more Novo and Lilly can ask for their GLP-1 products.

Here is where the governments jump in. They also see these huge GLP-1 benefits, but want to make sure the system benefits most. Obesity is one of the most costly diseases for our healthcare system and so the governments regulate the drug only for obesity use.

How can this change?

Patents will expire and other companies will find ways to bypass the patents or create their own. Pfizer and Roche are both working on their own GLP-1 products.

In other words, the supply gets bigger -> price of the drug will come down -> and governments can ease the prescriptions.

First, governments will just widen the prescriptions to more diseases, to not let the demand side surge again. But after a couple of years, I believe that you won't need a prescription anymore.

Andrew Dudum expects competition to push prices from $1,500 / month toward $50 / month as supply grows & patents expire.

Who benefits from this change?

The one who can get the GLP-1 products to the customer. As long as the products are protected by prescriptions, $HIMS basically has a monopoly.

They will need to do everything in their power to attract as many customers as possible to the platform with this monopoly.

They will need to be the front-tier supplier/platform when prescriptions fall off. If not, it will be easy for Amazon or others to catch up.

The $500 billion space economy isn't constrained by rocket fuel, but by constrained by radiation. BAE Systems, $BAESY, is the overlooked architect solving this microscopic chokepoint.

To understand the bottleneck, we have to look at the environment. The space economy is fundamentally constrained by radiation. Earth's magnetic field protects terrestrial data centers, but once a satellite reaches orbit or deep space, it is bombarded by trapped protons in the Van Allen belts, galactic cosmic rays, and solar flares.

When high-energy particles strike a standard commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) semiconductor, they cause single-event upsets or total ionizing dose degradation (which eventually fries the chip completely). 

A $500 million satellite with a standard silicon processor will become dead space debris in a matter of days or weeks. To survive, the electronics must be heavily modified through a process called radiation hardening by design (RHBD) or manufactured on specialized insulating substrates.

The barrier to entry in rad-hard compute is not just technological; it is deeply institutional. BAE Systems dominates this chokepoint due to three compounding factors:

1. The heritage Premium: In the aerospace industry, risk tolerance is zero. Space agencies and commercial operators rely on flight heritage, meaning they only want to buy components that have already proven they can survive in space. 

BAE’s flagship processor, the RAD750, has supported over 200 space missions, including powering NASA's Mars rovers (Perseverance, Curiosity) and the James Webb Space Telescope.

2. Insane Qualification Cycles: Testing a chip for space readiness is excruciating. It involves years of subjecting processors to heavy ion accelerators and extreme thermal vacuums to meet rigorous military and space standards (like MIL-PRF-38535). New entrants cannot simply spin up a startup to compete.

3. Geopolitical and Export Moats: Rad-hard manufacturing is heavily scrutinized under export controls. BAE Systems, deeply entrenched in the US and UK defense apparatus, has the trusted foundry partnerships (such as their collaboration with GlobalFoundries) and security clearances required to manufacture these chips at scale.

Conclusion
The space economy is transitioning. We are seeing a massive increase in demand for edge computing in space, satellites that can process AI, optical sensor data, and secure communications directly in orbit rather than beaming raw data back to Earth.

This requires vastly more computational power than legacy satellites. BAE's transition from the legacy RAD750 to their newer, high-performance RAD510 and RAD5545 System-on-Chips positions them perfectly.

Because foundry capacity for rad-hard wafers is structurally limited globally, BAE's existing pipeline and deep integration with foundries make them a pure bottleneck. If a commercial or government entity wants to launch a complex, long-duration asset, they are almost certainly waiting in BAE Systems' backlog to get their central computer.

SK Hynix still looks like a clear buying opportunity to me. 

This graph perfectly shows why. Despite their stock price running up, their earnings growth is so explosive that the valuation keeps compressing. 

Every time the Forward P/E spikes, they report massive revenues and raise guidance, crushing the P/E ratio back down. Right now, they are trading at a Forward P/E of roughly 5.37.

They will report earnings at the end of April, and I expect this cycle to repeat. 

Competitors like Samsung and $MU trade at a Forward P/E of 8.38 and 10.17. 

Hynix has a clear valuation advantage against those two, and it all stems from their monopoly over $NVDA's HBM supply. 

Let me explain

Nvidia’s GPUs are incredibly fast at processing data, but traditional memory chips couldn't feed them data quickly enough. This bottleneck is known as the 'memory wall'.

The solution was HBM. Instead of placing memory chips flat next to the processor, HBM stacks multiple ultra-thin DRAM memory dies vertically, right on top of each other.  

To make them communicate, engineers punch thousands of microscopic holes straight through the silicon layers and fill them with copper. These are called Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs). It creates a massive, multi-lane superhighway directly into the GPU, solving the bandwidth problem.

But stacking 8, 12, or 16 microscopic layers of silicon generates an immense amount of heat, and the physical pressure required to bond them together can easily crack or warp the ultra-thin dies. This is exactly where SK Hynix pulled ahead of the pack.

The core technical reason for SK Hynix's monopoly comes down to how they glue those stacked chips together.

For a long time, the industry standard was a process called TC-NCF (Thermal Compression with Non-Conductive Film). Samsung stuck with this method. It involves placing a thin, solid film between each layer of silicon and applying heavy pressure and heat to melt it and bond the chips. 

The problem? 

As the stacks got taller (moving to 12 and 16 layers), that film acted like a thermal blanket. It trapped the heat inside the chip. Furthermore, the intense physical pressure required to bond taller stacks frequently warped the fragile silicon, leading to massive defect rates.

SK Hynix, however, collaborated with Japanese materials companies to pioneer a totally different approach called MR-MUF (Mass Reflow Molded Underfill). 

Instead of solid films and heavy pressure, SK Hynix stacks the chips, momentarily melts all the metallic connections at once, and then injects a specialized liquid epoxy molding compound into the microscopic gaps between the layers before hardening it.

This liquid epoxy has roughly twice the thermal conductivity of the traditional films, meaning heat dissipates beautifully. Because it's injected as a liquid, it requires far less physical pressure, completely eliminating the warping issues that plagued Samsung.

As a result, SK Hynix was able to achieve manufacturing yields approaching 90%, while competitors struggling with the older film methods were reportedly stuck around 60% to 70%. When $NVDA needs millions of flawless chips, they go to the manufacturer that doesn't throw a third of them in the trash.

Ultimately, Samsung and $MU are playing catch-up today because they blinked during the lean years. SK Hynix co-developed the original HBM standards back in 2013 and stubbornly continued funding the R&D even when the technology was losing money. 

Samsung actually disbanded its dedicated HBM team in 2019 because the market seemed too niche. When the generative AI boom suddenly hit in 2023, SK Hynix was the only manufacturer on the planet with a mature, high-yield, battle-tested packaging process ready to supply Nvidia's voracious appetite.

February Portfolio Recap

February Performance: -15.6%
Year-to-Date (YTD) Performance: -0.9%

If you only looked at February, you might think the sky was falling. A -15.6% drop in a single month sounds brutal on paper. 

But as investors, we have to zoom out. 

My YTD performance is basically flat at -0.9%. 
What does that tell us? 
It tells us that January was a massive, euphoric run-up, and February was simply the market digesting those gains.

Here is a look under the hood at what happened this month, and why my conviction remains unchanged.

1. The Valuation Reset in AI & Software

The biggest drag on the portfolio this month came from my highest-conviction tech and software names: $PLTR, $CRWD, $NET. 

Did the fundamentals of these businesses break? Absolutely not. Many of them reported stellar earnings, massive revenue growth, and expanding free cash flow. 

But when stocks are priced for perfection, the market will eventually force a multiple compression. Institutional investors took their profits after a hot start to the year, and valuations simply took a breather. The underlying businesses are executing flawlessly.

2. The High-Beta Edge

This portfolio is intentionally designed for aggressive, disruptive growth. Holdings like $PL, $RKLB, $IREN, $TMDX, $HIMS, $HOOD, $FLNC, and $AMPX are high-beta by nature.

When the market is in a risk-on mood, these names fly. When the market pivots to risk-off, they pull back disproportionately. Volatility is simply the price of admission for owning the next generation of market leaders.

3. The Anchors Doing Their Job

It wasn't all extreme volatility. My semiconductor and foundational holdings: $ASML, $ASMI, $HOLN, $NU and $GOOGL remained resilient. These companies provide som structural, low-beta support that kept the total YTD drawdown near zero while the tech sector repriced itself.

The Strategy Going Forward: Masterly Inactivity

I didn't make a single trade this month. No panic selling, no chasing trends, no trying to time the bottom.

Doing nothing is an active choice. When you own a concentrated basket of highly disruptive companies, the worst thing you can do is interrupt compounding because of a 30-day sentiment shift. 

The portfolio is built for the long term, the theses for these 16 companies are intact, and I am perfectly comfortable letting the businesses do the heavy lifting while the market sorts out its feelings.
