My take on the production problems at $EOSE and $FLNC, and mainly, why there is a major difference. 

The energy storage sector is experiencing exponential demand right now, driven by utility-scale renewable projects and the rise of power-hungry AI data centers. However, scaling up hardware production remains a capital-intensive and operationally fraught challenge.

Based on the latest quarterly filings from Fluence Energy   and Eos Energy Enterprises, both companies are facing production and margin headwinds. Yet, the nature and severity of these problems are vastly different.

Eos Energy: The Automation Struggle
Eos Energy’s Q4 2025 earnings report delivered a harsh reality check, sending the stock plummeting. While the company achieved a record $114.2 million in full-year revenue, it severely missed its Q4 revenue targets, bringing in $58 million against a forecasted $92.8 million.

The core of Eos's struggle lies in its ambitious initiative to scale its novel aqueous zinc-halide battery manufacturing.

Management pointed to significant challenges in achieving quality targets on their new automated bipolar production lines.

The inability to maintain consistent quality off the automated line has resulted in high equipment downtime, isolated supplier non-conformances, extensive product rework, and ultimately, lost revenue that missed Q4 guidance.

While $EOSE touted a margin improvement, the reality is that their 2025 gross loss was a massive $143.8 million. It currently costs Eos significantly more to build their batteries than they can sell them for.

Fluence Energy: Hiccups on a Profitable Path
Fluence’s Q1 FY2026 earnings also shocked the market, though for entirely different reasons. The company delivered a massive 154% year-over-year revenue surge to $475.2 million but saw its adjusted gross margin shrink to 5.6%, well below its 11%–13% target.

However, Fluence’s production and margin issues are tied to discrete contract execution rather than fundamental technology scaling problems.

The bulk of the margin compression was tied to $20 million in extra, project-specific costs stemming from scope and schedule changes on two non-U.S. projects.

$FLNC has also dealt with a slower-than-expected production ramp at its recently commissioned U.S. manufacturing facilities, but management noted that module production is now running ahead of plan.

Management noted that corrective actions are already in place, domestic cell supply chains are secured for the year, and they fully expect to recover the discrete contract costs from their customers.

The fundamental difference
If you look at the raw stock reactions, both companies were heavily penalized by the market following their respective earnings calls. However, a deeper look at their financial health shows that Fluence's situation is a temporary operational hurdle, while Eos is fighting a structural battle for survival.

When comparing their recent filings directly, the stark contrast in financial health becomes obvious. Fluence generated $475.2 million in revenue over its latest quarter while maintaining a positive 5.6% adjusted gross margin, backed by a robust $1.1 billion in total liquidity.

In contrast, Eos reported just $58 million in revenue for Q4 2025, falling well short of forecasts, and posted a staggering full-year net loss of $969.6 million. Eos continues to operate with deep negative gross margins and relies heavily on complex financing, equity dilution, and debt to maintain its $625 million cash position.

The distinction is clear: Fluence's products are structurally profitable. Even with a disappointing quarter, they make a gross profit on what they sell. Eos, on the other hand, is still trying to figure out how to manufacture its proprietary tech at scale without losing money on every unit that rolls off the line.

The Verdict: Why I Choose Fluence Over EOS Energy
For investors weighing the energy storage sector, Fluence offers a much more compelling and de-risked value proposition compared to Eos Energy.

Fluence is a battery-agnostic systems integrator relying primarily on proven lithium-ion technology. Their primary challenge is supply chain management and contract execution. Eos is trying to commercialize a totally new zinc-based chemistry via complex, untested automated manufacturing.

Fluence is also sitting on a record $5.5 billion backlog, which fully covers the midpoint of their entire $3.4 billion revenue guidance for fiscal 2026. Eos's backlog sits at $701.5 million, and their revenue visibility is constantly threatened by their inability to get functional product out the door on time.

Eos's massive 2025 net loss of nearly $1 billion (though largely driven by non-cash items) highlights a highly speculative business model that requires constant capital injections. Fluence operates from a position of strength with $1.1 billion in liquidity and a clear, reaffirmed line of sight toward adjusted EBITDA profitability for the year.

Ultimately, $FLNC is a maturing market leader dealing with the growing pains of a massive global backlog. $EOSE is an early-stage speculative play still trying to prove its factory can build a profitable product. With $FLNC at $2.86B market cap and $EOSE at $2B market cap, this is an easy decision for me.

Why I think you should be careful buying this SaaS dip.

Today, during our bi-weekly management meeting, we discussed cost-cutting measures. This is nothing new, as things aren't going superbly in our business right now.

We are a Scandinavian company, so cutting jobs isn't in our DNA. We believe that if we remain loyal to our employees, they will repay us with loyalty and trust when the market picks up.

So, we often look at other measures. And today, for the first time, there was a new topic on the agenda: our ERP system.

Let me explain.

An ERP system is a hassle for every sales employee and a lovely tool for management. Managers can pull lists of won, lost, or stalled opportunities, competitors, quotes, market share... as long as the sales employees fill everything in correctly.

That's the hassle: correctly.

They have to fill in every box correctly, link every opportunity with a quote correctly, link the competitors correctly,... you know the drill. This takes time, it's repetitive and boring.

Time-consuming, repetitive, and boring.

Sounds like an ideal job for AI.

$CRM thought exactly the same. In 2014, Salesforce started investing in a project now known as Salesforce Einstein, which is the AI layer on top of the standard Salesforce platform.

Since 2014, the project has cost approximately $40B. Yet, according to the latest results, Salesforce Einstein brought in $800M in revenue in 2026...

Two years ago, we thought Einstein would be a huge benefit. AI would make analysis way easier, and it truly does today.

There is just one major problem: AI has evolved. Einstein has been outpaced.

We feel that with most basic LLMs today, it no longer matters where the information is stored. The bot will find it. It doesn't matter if sales reps store the competitor info perfectly, link the quote perfectly, or close an opportunity correctly. AI will just find the data.

The most expensive ERP systems still haven't solved this hassle, while easy-to-access AI tools have. Even a combination of Microsoft Dynamics and Copilot (which isn't universally seen as the best LLM) would already solve this problem partially.

At the moment, we haven't changed our systems. I don't think we will for a long time. But it highlights a major $40B issue.

AI has disrupted major businesses, is disrupting major businesses, and will continue to disrupt businesses.

I'm not saying that none of the SaaS companies can make a comeback. Today was just a major reality check for me.

They are not the safe havens they used to be. You can't just park your money in these companies without being deeply aware of the impact of AI.

Investing is not about what you want to happen, but about what is really happening. So open your eyes, listen, and always do your research.

The safest bets of today can be major risks tomorrow.

$EOSE completely missed earnings today. Dropping 38% as a result. Here is my take on the company. 

The Opportunity

$EOSE is an American manufacturer that designs and builds stationary, long-duration battery energy storage systems primarily for utility, commercial, and industrial applications. 

Eos uses a proprietary Znyth aqueous zinc-halide chemistry that is completely non-flammable and non-toxic.  Because AI hyperscale data centers require massive, uninterrupted power without the severe fire risks and zoning hurdles of traditional lithium-ion batteries, Eos is uniquely positioned to supply this booming sector.

By sourcing 94% of their materials (like bulk zinc and titanium) within the United States, they are shielded from global supply chain shocks and perfectly positioned to harvest lucrative government subsidies.

The Risk

Despite the explosive revenue growth, $EOSE is losing money on every single battery it sells. They ended December 2025 with a gross margin of -93.83% and a free cash flow margin of -129.73%. They are burning cash at a staggering rate and absolutely must cross the gross margin breakeven point by late 2026 or 2027 to survive long-term.

To keep their operations running and retain elite engineering talent without draining all their cash, management relies heavily on Stock-Based Compensation (SBC). In 2025, non-cash items (mostly SBC) accounted for a staggering $746.8 million of their net loss. This acts as a permanent, ongoing drag on the value of the shares you hold.

The company's future hinges entirely on Project AMAZE, their aggressive plan to scale robotic manufacturing to an 8 gigawatt-hour annual capacity by 2027.  Analysts warn there is zero margin for error. Any minor supply chain bottleneck or failure in automated robotic cycle times will result in catastrophic cash burn.

Eos has a history of manufacturing struggles, including a flawed early strategy in China and a painful, costly transition from their Gen 2.3 to Z3 modules that resulted in millions of dollars in write-downs. Furthermore, traditional lithium-ion still holds 70% of the market. If global lithium prices crash, Eos's cost advantages could evaporate overnight.

My conclusion

Ultimately, despite the undeniable potential of their zinc-halide technology in the AI and renewable energy sectors, I wouldn't buy $EOSE at this moment. 

The transition from a promising R&D concept to a reliable commercial manufacturer requires a level of flawless execution that management has simply not demonstrated. 

This quarter, they actively missed their own full-year revenue expectations and admitted to a critical five-week delay in hitting their 2 gigawatt-hour production capacity milestone. 

When a company is in such a fragile, capital-intensive phase of scaling, these are not just minor hiccups but they are glaring red flags that erode trust in leadership's ability to deliver on their aggressive operational roadmaps.

Not financial advice, just my opinion.

I got some questions regarding the competitors of $PL and how they protect margins. Here is my view, which is mainly economic.

1. SpaceX

I think SpaceX is a threat for every space company as they have everything. You are comparing an $8B company to a (potentially) $1.5T company, so of course Planet won't overtake SpaceX.

There are a few things why I think Planet will keep growing despite the pressure of SpaceX.

- Planet has a lot of historical data, which SpaceX has not. So if you want to do a historical analysis on a certain region, the data of Planet has to be used.

- They are only fighting over defensive contracts. Those defensive contracts are 60% of Planet's revenue (and the highest growing segment), but 40% of the revenues of Planet comes from the environmental sector, sustainability sector, private sector,... SpaceX has no interest in competing on that 40%.

- SpaceX's Earth observation network is a highly classified military project built exclusively for U.S. intelligence agencies. The government can't share any of the information with the outside world. They shared Planet's pictures as proof for "Operation Midnight Hammer" for example. They will always need the data of $PL.

- The most important part is that they actually operate best together on the defensive part. Planet scans the entire world 24/7, SpaceX does not do this. SpaceX does a specific task in a specific region. Planet also works on a SaaS business model, SpaceX operates on specific projects. 

The government wants to scan the entire world to make sure they find all potential threats. They use Planet's images and AI to find potential threats. Once they identify a potential threat, they might use the more sophisticated technology of SpaceX to scan that region or do a specific task in that region.

- To make it easy, I compare this a bit with the music industry. You use Spotify (Planet) to scan the whole industry and for daily listening. You pay a (small) fee every month to listen to every artist in the world. Once you find a great artist, you want to see that artist live. Spotify can't give you that experience, so you buy a ticket to a concert (SpaceX). Instead of paying a monthly fee, you pay once (normally a bigger fee than the monthly fee) for that concert.

2. Satellogic

$SATL is actually trying to be the biggest disruptor of Planet Labs. Their satellites are working at a better resolution than the satellites of Planet. While Planet is trying to close the resolution gap with Satellogic, it looks like they can't fully close this gap.

Why I think Planet will stay superior

- Planet has a huge head start. They make a daily scan of the entire globe. They have around 180 SuperDoves in LEO. Satellogic only has 50 NewSats, which is roughly enough to scan the entire globe every 2 weeks.

To scan the entire Earth daily they will need around 150 more NewSats. $SATL missed their first target to have 200 NewSats in LEO, which was targeted in 2025. The new target is 2027, although sources indicate that 2029 will be more realistic.

- While $SATL will have to burn through cash for at least 4 more years, $PL recorded 3 positive cash flow quarters in a row already. They are using this cash to innovate their profit-making fleet. Satellogic will have to use every dollar to launch as many satellites as possible.

- Like SpaceX, Satellogic can only compete on defense contracts. Planet has acquired software and AI companies to translate their images into ready-to-use data feeds. 

Instead of selling a farmer a picture of a field and making them figure it out, Planet directly sells them a data feed of soil water content or crop biomass. Satellogic is still primarily focused on selling the raw images.

- Planet doesn't just email a JPEG to a customer. Their data is directly piped into the internal software systems of the U.S. government, NATO, and massive agricultural corporations via APIs. 

Once a major intelligence agency or a massive company like Bayer integrates Planet's data feeds into their daily, automated workflows, the switching cost is astronomically high. Even if Satellogic offers a slightly cheaper or sharper image, tearing out the foundational data plumbing of an entire intelligence agency to switch providers is a nightmare most customers won't do.

This is just my take. This is not financial advice, do your own research.

Most investors look at Planet Labs and see satellites. They see capital expenditure. They see launch risks.

They are missing the forest for the trees.

Planet Labs is not a normal space company. Planet Labs is a SaaS Database company with cameras in orbit.

Here is the thesis for $PL based strictly on the fundamentals and the unique economics revealed in their 10-Ks and 10-Qs.

1. The One-to-Many Economics (The Margin Story)
This is the single most important concept in the Planet Labs bull case, and it’s buried in their Description of Business filings.

Traditional space companies (like Maxar or BlackSky) operate on a Tasking model.

- Customer wants a photo.
- Satellite moves.
- Photo taken.
- Result: 1 Unit of Cost = 1 Unit of Revenue.

Planet operates on a Monitoring model (Always-on).

The constellation scans the entire landmass of Earth daily.

The data goes into the database.

Customer A (Agriculture) buys the data.
Customer B (Defense) buys the exact same data.
Customer C (Finance) buys the exact same data.

The Unit Economics: You pay for the satellite once. You sell the same pixel infinite times. This is why their Gross Margins are expanding toward software levels (aiming for 70%+ long-term targets), vastly superior to traditional aerospace hardware margins.

2. The Unreplicable Moat: The Time Machine
In their Annual Reports, Planet highlights their proprietary archive.

Competitors are launching satellites today. Great. They can show you what the world looks like today.

But if an intelligence agency needs to know "When did China start building this runway?" or a hedge fund needs to know "How has this crop yield changed since 2018?", only Planet Labs has the answer.

They have an image of every spot on Earth, every day, going back years.

Competitor Lag: 10+ years.

Barrier to Entry: Impossible. You cannot launch a satellite today to take a picture of yesterday.

This archive is the training data for the world's geospatial AI. You cannot train a model on change-detection without historical data. $PL owns the training set.

3. Financial Stability (The Anti-SPAC)
While the space sector is littered with bankruptcies (Virgin Orbit, Astra), look at the Balance Sheet from the latest filings:

Cash & Cash Equivalents: Significant liquidity (approx ~$200M-$300M range depending on the specific quarter, usually ~30% of market cap).

Debt: Negligible to zero.

They are not desperate for cash. They are playing the long game while competitors starve.

4. The Quality of Revenue
Reviewing the Key Business Metrics in their filings reveals why this is a high-quality asset:

Recurring ACV (Annual Contract Value): Consistently >90%.
This implies their revenue is sticky. Once a government or agricultural giant integrates Planet data into their workflow, they don't churn. It becomes a utility like electricity.

Net Dollar Retention (NDR): Frequently >100%.
Existing customers aren't just staying; they are spending more every year.

5. The Sleeping Giant: Government Contracts

The 10-K highlights a shift in strategy: From Data to Solutions.

We are seeing a massive transition in US Government (USG) spending. The NRO (National Reconnaissance Office) and NGA (National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency) are moving from buying satellites to buying commercial data.

EOCL Contract: A multi-year validation by the NRO.
NASA: Renewed and expanded usage.

Planet is already embedded in the US federal ecosystem. As geopolitical tensions rise (Ukraine, Middle East, Taiwan Strait), the demand for "Daily, Global Transparency" becomes inelastic.

The Valuation Disconnect

The market treats $PL like a speculative de-SPAC. But the filings show a company with:

SaaS metrics (90%+ recurring revenue).
Tech monopoly (Daily scan).
Fortress balance sheet (High cash, no debt).

The Catalyst: The launch of the Pelican (high-res) and Tanager (hyperspectral) constellations.

Pelican closes the resolution gap with Maxar.

Tanager opens a new market in carbon/methane detection (ESG compliance).

Summary:
You are buying a monopoly on daily Earth data for roughly the price of the cash on their books plus a small premium. When the market realizes this is an AI/Data play and not a Hardware play, the multiple expansion will be violent.

$PL has surged with almost 500% in 2025. I'll explain why it has performed so well and which key milestones Planet reached in 2025.

1. Data Breakthroughs: Planet significantly upgraded the eyes of its fleet to provide more precise information.

The Tanager Hyperspectral Satellite now captures the full light spectrum (VSWIR), allowing users to identify the exact chemical cause of a problem, such as specific gas emissions, rather than just seeing visual changes.

Planet also sharpened its Planetary Variables, boosting Crop Biomass resolution to 3 meters, Soil Water and Land Surface Temperature to 20 meters, providing 25 times the clarity for soil and thermal analysis.

2. Platform & Workflow Optimization: The focus was on making geospatial data easier to manage without needing massive local storage.

Planet streamlined its platform by consolidating tools like Sentinel Hub into a single, unified experience at insight.planet. They also focused on cloud-native GIS workflows, updating the ArcGIS Pro Add-in so professionals can stream imagery instantly and manage data in the cloud without the burden of downloading massive local files.

Through a partnership with SkyFi, the company introduced Planet Select, a flexible pay-as-you-go portal for on-demand access to high-resolution SkySat imagery.

3. Automated AI solutions: New AI-driven tools were launched to handle data at a massive scale.

Planet introduced machine learning solutions like Global Aircraft Detection, which monitors thousands of airfields daily to identify trends and anomalies.

For the agricultural sector, the new Planet Area Monitoring Service (AMS) now automates compliance and verification across millions of hectares using a simple traffic light system. This automated approach replaces slow, manual field inspections with objective, field-level signals, significantly reducing costs and accelerating impact for geospatial professionals worldwide.

4. Ambitious Projects: Planet entered into two landmark partnerships that define the future of space-based infrastructure.

Project Suncatcher is a research collaboration with $GOOGL. Planet is helping to build prototype satellites designed to host AI data centers in orbit, leveraging near-constant solar power to run massive machine learning workloads in space.

$PL signed a massive $230 million agreement with Sky Perfect JSAT to build and launch a dedicated low-Earth orbit constellation using Planet’s next-generation Pelican satellites. This partnership marks a major move into the space intelligence and defense markets, providing high-resolution, 30cm-class imagery to support national security and disaster prevention initiatives.

The 10 Most Undervalued Quality Companies of 2026 according to the reverse DCF!

Each year I run a reverse DCF analysis on around 250 companies. The goal of a reverse DCF is to see how much free cash flow growth the market is pricing in. I compare these to the 10- 5- and 3- Year FCF CAGR to see if investors are expecting the company to do worse or better than the previous years.

There are 3 rules:
1. The FCF should be positive in at least 8 of the last 10 years.
2. The FCF should be positive in the last year.
3. The standard deviation of the FCF should be less than 40%.
